findings.title: Detach background writes from request cancellation
findings.body: All four asynchronous legacy writes derive their timeout context from the original request context. That context is canceled when the HTTP handler completes, and WithTimeoutCause does not remove the parent's cancellation or deadline. Because these methods return immediately, legacy writes can be canceled before they start or finish despite the successful unified-storage response. Preserve the request context's values but detach its cancellation before applying the background timeout.

findings.title: Mirror the committed update instead of replaying UpdatedObjectInfo
findings.body: Legacy.Update now receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo rather than a wrapper around the object successfully committed to unified storage. For PATCH operations, UpdatedObjectInfo computes the new object from the backend's existing object. Since asynchronous legacy storage can lag or have missed an earlier write, replaying the patch can produce different content—for example, a title-only patch can preserve an obsolete interval in legacy. Pass the committed result through an appropriate update wrapper so the backup receives the same resource state.

findings.title: Preserve write ordering when mirroring to legacy storage
findings.body: Each successful write starts an independent goroutine, with no ordering between legacy operations on the same resource. A client can successfully create a resource and then delete it, but the legacy delete can execute before the legacy create; the ignored NotFound error is then followed by creation of a record that no longer exists in unified storage. Successive updates can similarly overwrite newer legacy state with older state. Use ordered replication or per-resource serialization rather than unrelated goroutines.

findings.title: Attribute duration and error samples to the correct backend
findings.body: The unified-storage failure branches in Create and Update call recordLegacyDuration, even though no legacy operation ran. Conversely, the asynchronous legacy DeleteCollection calls recordStorageDuration at line 166. This attributes unified failures to legacy and legacy collection-delete failures to unified storage, making the backend latency/error metrics misleading. Record each sample against the backend that performed the operation.

findings.title: Do not use resource names as the duration metric's kind label
findings.body: The successful unified Delete records its duration using name where the other calls pass options.Kind. This creates a distinct metric label value for every deleted resource name instead of grouping samples by kind. As deletion volume grows, retained metric series and scrape overhead can grow without bound, while successful and failed deletes are also grouped inconsistently. Pass the kind rather than the resource name.

findings.title: Distinguish the two backends and verify asynchronous mirroring
findings.body: The legacy and unified mocks share the same mock.Mock and use identical method expectation names, so an expectation configured for one backend can satisfy a call to the other. For example, the Create unified-failure case configures only setupLegacyFn but still exercises the unified failure path through that shared expectation. The write tests also neither await nor assert the background legacy calls, so removing legacy mirroring entirely would leave them passing. Use independent backend mocks and explicitly await and verify successful mirroring and the absence of legacy writes after unified failures.
